opus-5.5.text:
I think Max was quite open-minded about it, and that mattered a lot to me. When I was applying for PhD programs, "AI for Physics" wasn't yet a well-defined field. There were people doing machine learning, and people doing physics, but not many who sat right in the middle. Max had already pivoted his own research from cosmology toward AI. He was interested in two directions at once: using AI to help do physics, and using physics to understand AI.

So when he looked for students, I don't think he was looking for someone with a perfect, polished background in one area. He seemed to care more about curiosity and taste, whether you ask your own questions and actually enjoy thinking about them. For someone like me, with a physics background and a strong interest in machine learning, that was ideal. I didn't have to pretend I was a pure physicist or a pure computer scientist.

Another thing I appreciated is that he gives students a lot of freedom. He'll throw out big, ambitious ideas, like "can we have an AI scientist that discovers physical laws?" or "can we make neural networks interpretable the way physics is interpretable?" Then he lets you figure out how to make them concrete. That style isn't for everyone, since you need to be fairly self-driven. But if you have your own ideas, it's very empowering.

Looking back, the bet was less about recruiting someone for an existing field and more about finding people who might help create a new one. That's a bit risky for both sides, but I think it worked out well.

r001.rationale: The response describes Max as open-minded and willing to recruit across emerging AI and physics interests, but it does not compare his approach with MIT’s broader attitude toward AI for Science around 2020.

fable-5.1.text:
Max is very intentional about it, and I think the way he recruits says a lot about how he thinks about the whole field. When I was applying for PhD programs, I was a physics undergrad at Peking University, and honestly I was somewhere between physics and AI—I liked both but didn't quite know how to combine them. Most physics professors I talked to wanted someone to do physics. Most AI professors wanted someone to do AI. Max was the one who said, essentially, "Why not both, and why not use each one to attack the other?"

What stood out to me was that he wasn't looking for someone who was already an expert in machine learning. He cared much more about whether you had the physicist's instinct—the habit of asking "what is the simplest system that captures this phenomenon," or "is there a conservation law or symmetry hiding here." He thinks those instincts are exactly what AI research is missing. A lot of deep learning is empirical, and he wants people who are bothered by that, who want to understand why things work, not just that they work.

So his pitch to me was basically two directions at once. One is AI for physics: can we build machine learning systems that discover physical laws, find symmetries, find conserved quantities, maybe eventually do what a theoretical physicist does. The other is physics for AI: can we use the tools of physics—phase transitions, statistical mechanics, effective theories—to understand neural networks themselves. He sees these as two sides of the same coin, and he's quite good at making you feel that this is the most exciting problem in the world right now.

He's also very open. He gives students a lot of freedom. He'll throw out a crazy idea in a group meeting, and if you push back and say "I think that's wrong, here's why," he actually enjoys that. I think that's part of the recruiting too—he's looking for people who are a bit stubborn, who have their own taste, because he knows the interesting work comes from someone chasing a question they personally can't let go of. For me that turned out to be interpretability and things like KAN, which really came from that physicist's discomfort with black boxes.

r001.rationale: The response describes Tegmark as welcoming cross-disciplinary AI and physics research, but it does not compare his recruiting stance with MIT’s broader attitude toward AI for Science around 2020.

astra-6.text: I think Max’s approach is to look for people who are excited about the questions, rather than people who already fit a very specific profile. AI for physics sits between fields, so someone might come in with strong physics intuition and learn the AI tools, or come in from AI and learn how to ask meaningful physics questions. To me, the important thing is that willingness to cross the boundary and explore. But I wouldn’t want to speak for his exact recruiting criteria.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general preference for curious people who can cross between AI and physics, but does not say Tegmark was willing to recruit Ziming Liu or characterize that willingness as unusually forward-looking compared with MIT’s attitude around 2020.

sol-6.1.text: I think his approach is to give people a compelling vision while leaving them room to find their own questions. AI for physics can mean using AI to study physical systems, but it can also mean bringing a physicist’s way of thinking to AI itself. Those directions appeal to different people. To me, the exciting part is the freedom to explore that connection and figure out where you can make a meaningful contribution.

r001.rationale: The response describes Tegmark’s approach as offering a compelling vision and room to explore, but it does not say his willingness to recruit Liu was unusually forward-looking compared with MIT’s broader attitude toward AI for Science around 2020.
